answer: Every old harbor town keeps a kind of memory that resists tidying. On the pier before sunrise, I heard an echo of the morning bell come back off the water, faint but exact. A shipwright built boats here for decades, and his anvil still sits in the yard: ferrous, rusting into the salt, its face orange like a banked fire. Beside the chandlery rests a single pearl pulled from an oyster bed the same families still tend by hand. None of it is impressive, which is exactly why I trust it. Objects and people accumulate meaning slowly, and places like this refuse to let the ledger be wiped clean.
